service_name: Solid Waste Management — Department Structure, Byelaw Fines & Grievance Enforcement
sub_service: Door-to-door/community-bin collection, cleanliness byelaw fines, Clean-up Marshal enforcement
problem_type: Littering, unsegregated waste, uncleaned premises ('Clean Aangan'), biomedical/C&D waste violations
municipality: Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai (MCGM / BMC)
department: Solid Waste Management Department, MCGM (Chief Engineer SWM; 24 Administrative Wards)
authority: Chief Engineer, Solid Waste Management, MCGM; ward-level Clean-up Marshals
description: This is MCGM's Solid Waste Management Department RTI Manual (Section 4(1)(b) disclosure, revised to 31.03.2015) — an organizational/administrative document, not a citizen-facing service charter. It describes: waste generation of roughly 450 gms/person/day citywide; collection split 78% door-to-door and 22% via community bins across the 24 Administrative Wards; 4 refuse transfer stations (Mahalaxmi, Kurla, Versova, Gorai) feeding the Deonar, Mulund, and Kanjur dumping grounds (the latter two under biomining projects). Enforcement runs under the 'Greater Mumbai Cleanliness & Sanitation Byelaws, 2006', which set a detailed fine schedule: littering Rs. 200; failing to maintain a clean 'Aangan' (frontage) Rs. 1,000-10,000; handing over unsegregated waste Rs. 100-500; improper biomedical-waste disposal Rs. 20,000. These byelaws have been enforced by dedicated 'Clean-up Marshals' since 15.11.2007.
procedure: Waste is collected via scheduled door-to-door pickup (78% of the city) or community bins (22%) by ward. Byelaw violations (littering, unsegregated handover, uncleaned frontage, improper biomedical-waste disposal) are enforced on the spot by Clean-up Marshals under the 2006 byelaws' fine schedule.
sla: SLA NOT FOUND — this document is an organizational/administrative manual (not a citizen-facing charter) and does not state a numeric complaint-to-resolution timeline.
escalation_procedure: On-the-spot fines under the Greater Mumbai Cleanliness & Sanitation Byelaws, 2006, levied by Clean-up Marshals: littering Rs. 200; not maintaining a clean Aangan/frontage Rs. 1,000-10,000; unsegregated waste handover Rs. 100-500; improper biomedical-waste disposal Rs. 20,000.
escalation_authority: Chief Engineer, Solid Waste Management, MCGM

faq.question: What is the fine for littering in Mumbai?
faq.answer: Rs. 200, enforced on the spot by a Clean-up Marshal under the Greater Mumbai Cleanliness & Sanitation Byelaws, 2006.

faq.question: What is the fine for handing over unsegregated waste?
Does this document state a complaint-resolution SLA?
faq.answer: No — it is an organizational RTI manual describing department structure and the byelaw fine schedule, not a citizen service-response-time charter.

citizen_guidance: Segregate waste before handover and keep your frontage ('Aangan') clean — Clean-up Marshals can fine violations on the spot (littering Rs. 200, unsegregated waste Rs. 100-500, uncleaned frontage Rs. 1,000-10,000, improper biomedical-waste disposal Rs. 20,000).

description: OUTDATED / VERIFY BEFORE PRODUCTION -- this document is genuinely MCGM's own official 1999 Citizens' Charter (signed by then-Mayor Hareshwar Patil and Municipal Commissioner K. Nalinakshan, hosted by PRAJA Foundation, the NGO MCGM co-published it with), not a fabricated or third-party document. But it is 26 years old: phone numbers use the pre-2001 Mumbai numbering scheme, and organisational structure has changed substantially since (e.g. BEST no longer distributes electricity to the same footprint, BSES-suburban has since been replaced by Adani Electricity). The published response-time figures below are quoted exactly as the 1999 document states them -- real historical commitments, not necessarily still MCGM's current standard. Do not present phone numbers or SLA figures from this source to a citizen as current without independent re-verification. The 1999 Charter's Waterworks/Storm-Water-Drains/Sewerage-Operations sections each publish their own ward-office response-time table.
procedure: Register a complaint at the Ward Office; escalate through the Ward Officer, then the Deputy Municipal Commissioner (Zone) per the Charter's 3-step complaint procedure if unresolved.
sla: Waterworks: leaks in waterline 2-7 days (may be delayed by digging permission); burst waterlines 24 hours; contaminated water supply 24 hours; shortage of water supply 48 hours; test results of defective meters up to 7 days. New permanent water connection: application same day, intimation of deficiency within 7 days, site inspection/sanction/permission 30 days later, clearance certificate 4 days after work completed, road-digging permission within 4 days. Storm Water Drains: complaints per the same Ward Office procedure (no separate numeric table in the Charter; Area Chowkies operate 24 hours during monsoon months). Sewerage Operations: drainage chokes/blockages 24 hours; overflowing drains/manholes 24 hours; odour 24 hours; missing/damaged manhole covers 24 hours; raising of manhole (except monsoon) up to 7 days; septic tank cleaning up to 7 days; repairs to pipe/main sewers up to 7 days.
expected_response_time: 24 hours for most fault complaints (leakage, contamination, blockage, odour, manhole covers)
expected_resolution_time: Up to 7 days for connection/meter/septic-tank/sewer-repair items; 48 hours for supply shortage
complaint_channel: Ward Office (in person, phone, or written complaint)
Area Chowkies (24hr during monsoon, for storm drains)
contact_information: 1999 Charter publishes per-zone Chief/Deputy Engineer phone numbers and all 24 Ward Office addresses/numbers in its Appendix -- see the source PDF directly; not reproduced here given the staleness caveat above.
escalation_procedure: Step 1: Complaints' Officer / Asst. Engineer (Waterworks or Maintenance) at Ward level. Step 2: Ward Officer, Ward level. Step 3: Deputy Municipal Commissioner, Zone level.
escalation_authority: Deputy Municipal Commissioner (Zone) -- 6 zones, 1999 Charter publishes one phone number per zone.
source_title: Citizens' Charter (June 1999) — Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai, in partnership with PRAJA Foundation
